questions.questionText: What's the difference between batch inference and real-time inference?
options: They are the same thing with different names
Batch inference runs predictions on a large input set on a schedule; real-time inference returns a prediction per live request within a strict latency budget
Batch inference is only used for image models
Real-time inference cannot use neural networks
questions.correctAnswer: Batch inference runs predictions on a large input set on a schedule; real-time inference returns a prediction per live request within a strict latency budget
questions.explanation: Batch inference fits cases where predictions don't need to be instantaneous (e.g. nightly recommendation precomputation), while real-time inference serves individual requests live, which is what most API endpoints (including LLM chat) require.

questions.questionText: Why is model monitoring specifically important, beyond standard server monitoring?
options: It isn't important, standard server monitoring covers everything
A model that's gotten worse usually doesn't throw an error — it just quietly makes worse predictions, which is much easier to miss than a crash
Model monitoring only tracks server uptime
questions.correctAnswer: A model that's gotten worse usually doesn't throw an error — it just quietly makes worse predictions, which is much easier to miss than a crash
questions.explanation: Data drift and performance degradation are silent failure modes — the system keeps responding normally while the actual quality of predictions declines, which requires dedicated monitoring to catch.

questions.questionText: What is a canary deployment, and why use one for a new model version?
options: Deploying to 100% of traffic immediately with no testing
Routing a small fraction of real traffic to the new version first, comparing its live behavior, and rolling out fully only once confirmed to perform well
A type of data drift detection algorithm
A method for compressing model file size
questions.correctAnswer: Routing a small fraction of real traffic to the new version first, comparing its live behavior, and rolling out fully only once confirmed to perform well
questions.explanation: Since offline evaluation doesn't always predict real-world behavior perfectly, canary rollouts limit the blast radius of a problematic new version while still testing it against genuine live traffic.
